fixes.now: Catalogue code 0-306-40615, typed with hyphens, is treated as the nine digits 030640615 because the software ignores hyphens, so it does get a check digit: the check digit comes to 2, the same as for 030640615, which means the case's claim that it gets none doesn't match the rules.

fixes.shown: A catalogue code with only 8 digits gets no check digit instead of an error.
fixes.said: No, it should still get a check digit, using just the 8 digits it has.
fixes.now: A catalogue code of only 8 digits is still a valid input and gets a check digit rather than an error: the last digit is weighted 2, the digits are weighted 9 down to 2, and the code gets the digit that brings the total to a multiple of 11, or 'X' if that digit would be 10. For example, '12345678' gets '0', and '00000000' gets '0'. The code is not left without a check digit, which would happen only for input that is not exactly 8 or 9 digits, such as 7 digits, 10 digits, letters, or a number with fewer than 8 digits; those return NULL.

fixes.shown: An empty catalogue code gets no check digit.
fixes.said: No, an empty code should still get a check digit, which is '0'.
fixes.now: An empty catalogue code does get a check digit: the software returns '0' (as text) for it, not NULL, because empty text counts as having nothing left after outer spaces and hyphens are ignored.

rules: Whenever bulk_price is given a unit price and a quantity of fewer than 10, it returns unit price times quantity with no discount.

Whenever bulk_price is given a quantity of 10 to 49, it takes 5% off the whole order (not just the units above 10), so 10 units at 100 cents cost 950. A larger quantity at the same unit price never costs less than a smaller one. If the discounted total would come out below what any smaller quantity costs, such as 9.99 units at 100 cents costing 999 (no discount) against 950 for 10 units, bulk_price returns that higher total instead (999 for 10 units here).

Whenever bulk_price is given a quantity of 100 or more, it takes 15% off the whole order. When it is given a quantity of 50 to 99, it takes 10% off the whole order. A larger quantity at the same unit price never costs less than a smaller one. If the discounted total would come out below what any smaller quantity costs, bulk_price returns the highest total of any smaller quantity instead. So 49 units at 100 cents cost 4655, and 50 units at 100 cents also cost 4655, not 4500 (the 10% off only gives a lower price once it beats that); 99 units at 100 cents cost 8910, and 100 units cost 8910, not 8500.
Whenever a bulk_price discount leaves a fraction of a cent, bulk_price rounds half a cent up to the next whole cent (15 cents x 10 units gives 143, 3 x 10 gives 29).
Whenever bulk_price is given a quantity of zero or less, or a negative unit price, it returns 0 rather than a negative or error value.
Whenever either input to bulk_price is NULL, empty text, or any text (even '100' or '5'), bulk_price returns NULL; only real numbers are accepted, and this check comes before the zero/negative rule.
Whenever bulk_price is given a fractional quantity or price and no discount applies, it drops the fraction of the total (10.5 cents x 3 gives 31, 100 x 9.99 gives 999, while 100 x 2.5 gives 250).

Whenever bulk_price is given a fractional quantity of 10 or more or a fractional unit price with a discount, the discount tier is judged on the exact quantity (10.5 counts as 10 or more) and the discounted total is rounded half up, though it may come back in decimal form such as 998.0.

Whenever late_fee is given an invoice that is 5 days late or fewer (including zero or negative days), the fee is 0, because the grace period is only 5 days. From more than 5 days late, the fee is charged under the period rules: 6 to 30 days late is one started 30-day period, so the fee is 2% of the invoice amount, with the minimum of 500 cents and the cap of 20% of the invoice amount. The cap always wins over the minimum: if 500 cents is more than the cap, the fee is the cap, in whole cents rounded down. A 100-dollar invoice that is exactly 30 days late therefore owes 500 cents.

Rule 10: Whenever late_fee is given an invoice, the fee is 2% of the invoice amount per started 30-day period, after a 5-day grace. An invoice that is 31 to 60 days late is two periods, so the percentage is 4% of the invoice amount, but the minimum then applies to that figure. The fee has a minimum of 500 cents and is capped at 20% of the invoice amount; the cap always wins over the minimum, so if 500 cents is more than the cap, the fee is the cap, in whole cents rounded down. A 100-dollar invoice that is exactly 60 days late therefore owes 500 cents, not 400, because 4% is 400 cents and the 500-cent minimum raises it (the cap of 2000 cents is not reached). In the same way, a 100-dollar invoice 61 days late owes 600 cents, because 6% is already above the minimum.

Whenever late_fee is given an invoice that is 61 or more days late, the fee is 2% of the whole invoice amount for each started 30-day period, so 61 to 90 days late is 6%, 91 to 120 days late is 8%, and so on, not in addition to the 4%. The fee has a minimum of 500 cents and a cap of 20% of the invoice amount; the cap always wins over the minimum, so if 500 cents is more than the cap, the fee is the cap, in whole cents rounded down.

Whenever a late_fee percentage leaves a fraction of a cent, late_fee rounds half a cent up before the minimum and the cap are applied, so 4% of 12 cents rounds to 0 and 4% of 13 cents rounds to 1. The minimum fee of 500 cents and the cap of 20% of the invoice amount then apply to the rounded figure: a rounded fee below 500 cents is raised to the 500-cent minimum, but the cap always wins over the minimum, so the fee never goes above 20% of the invoice amount, taken in whole cents rounded down. A small invoice that is more than 5 days late therefore does not owe no fee; it owes the cap. For example, a 12-cent invoice 31 days late owes 2 cents and a 13-cent invoice 31 days late also owes 2 cents. (An invoice amount of zero or less still owes 0, as in rule 13.)
Whenever late_fee is given an invoice amount of zero or less, the fee is 0, whatever the days late.

Whenever late_fee is given a fractional days_late, it applies the same limits to the exact value (30.5 days is already in the 4% band, 60.5 days in the 6% band), and a fractional amount gives a whole-cent fee: the percentage is rounded half a cent up to a whole cent (100.5 cents at 4% rounds to 4), and the minimum of 500 cents and the cap of 20% of the invoice amount are then applied to that rounded figure, exactly as for any other invoice, with the cap always winning over the minimum and the cap taken in whole cents rounded down.
Whenever either input to late_fee is NULL, empty text or text of any kind (even '1000' or '40'), late_fee returns NULL, even when the amount is zero or the days are negative.
Whenever loyalty_tier is given fewer than 0 points (a negative balance), it returns 'suspended'. Whenever loyalty_tier is given 0 up to 999.9 points, it returns 'bronze'; this includes 0 and 999.9.
Whenever loyalty_tier is given 1000 to 4999 points (4999.5 included), it returns 'silver'; exactly 1000 is silver.

Whenever loyalty_tier is given 20000 points or more, it returns 'platinum'. Whenever loyalty_tier is given 5000 points or more but fewer than 20000 points, it returns 'gold'; exactly 5000 is gold and exactly 20000 is platinum.
Whenever loyalty_tier is given NULL, empty text or any text (even '5000'), it returns NULL.

Whenever make_slug is given a title, it lowercases it and turns every run of characters that are not English letters a-z or digits 0-9 (spaces, punctuation, underscores, slashes, hyphens) into a single hyphen, and removes hyphens from the start and end ('  Hello,   World!! ' becomes 'hello-world').

Whenever a title contains accented or non-English letters, make_slug does not transliterate them but treats them as separators ('Café Crème' becomes 'caf-cr-me'), and a title with no a-z or digits at all, or an empty title, gives empty text.

Whenever make_slug is given a maxlen, it cuts the slug to at most that many characters, but it never leaves a word cut in half. If the cut falls in the middle of a word (the character just after the cut is not a hyphen), it backs up to the last hyphen before the cut and drops everything from that hyphen on. If there is no hyphen to back up to (the slug is a single word), it keeps the plain cut. It then removes any hyphen left at the end ('Hello World' with maxlen 6 gives 'hello', 'Hello World Today' with maxlen 8 gives 'hello', and 'Hello World' with maxlen 1 gives 'h' because there is no hyphen to back up to).

Whenever make_slug is given a maxlen of zero or less, it returns 'untitled'; whenever it is given a maxlen that is empty text or text that is not a number, it returns empty text; a numeric text such as '5' works as 5 and a fractional maxlen such as 5.9 is cut down to 5.

Whenever make_slug is given a NULL maxlen, or no length limit at all, it returns NULL whatever the title, and it applies no slug-making or length limit; a NULL title also returns NULL whatever the maxlen.
Whenever make_slug is given a number as the title, it uses the number's text (12345 becomes '12345', 1.5 becomes '1-5').

Whenever isbn_check is given exactly 9 digits, it multiplies the digits by 10, 9, 8 ... 2 from left to right, adds them, and returns the digit that brings the total to a multiple of 11; if that digit would be 10 it returns 'X'; the result is text ('030640615' gives '2', '123456789' gives 'X', '000000000' gives '0'). Whenever it is given exactly 8 digits, it uses just those 8 digits in the same way, but the weights run 9, 8, 7 ... 2 from left to right (so the last digit is always multiplied by 2), then adds them and returns the digit that brings the total to a multiple of 11, or 'X' if that digit would be 10; the result is text ('00000000' gives '0', '12345678' gives '0').

Whenever isbn_check is given a code with leading or trailing spaces around 8 or 9 digits, it ignores those outer spaces. It also ignores hyphens anywhere in the code, so '0-306-40615' is treated as '030640615' and gets '2'. Spaces inside the code still make it invalid.

Whenever isbn_check is given anything other than exactly 8 or exactly 9 ASCII digits (once outer spaces and hyphens are ignored), it returns NULL, with one exception: empty text, or text with only hyphens or spaces (nothing left once outer spaces and hyphens are ignored), gets the check digit '0' (as text). Everything else still returns NULL, such as 7 or 10 digits, letters including an X, spaces inside the code, non-Western digits, or NULL (a NULL input still returns NULL).

Whenever isbn_check is given a whole number of 8 or 9 digits (123456789, 30640615), it treats it as text of those digits and works as for text of that length, with no leading zero added; a number with fewer than 8 digits (3064061) or a decimal such as 30640615.0 returns NULL, with no leading zero added.

Whenever fiscal_label is given a valid YYYY-MM-DD date, the fiscal year starts on 1 April and is named for the calendar year it ends in, so 2024-04-01 is 'FY2025-Q1' and 2025-03-26 is 'FY2025-Q4'. The last five days of the fiscal year, 27 to 31 March, are the year-end close and are labelled 'FY' plus the fiscal year, then '-CLOSE', so 2025-03-31 is 'FY2025-CLOSE'.

Whenever fiscal_label is given a date, quarters run Q1 April-June, Q2 July-September, Q3 October-December and Q4 1 January to 26 March, so 2024-06-30 is Q1, 2024-07-01 is Q2, 2024-10-01 is Q3, 2025-01-01 is Q4 and 2025-03-26 is Q4; the label looks like 'FY2025-Q1'. In every year, 27 to 31 March is the year-end close and is not part of Q4: those dates get the label 'FY2025-CLOSE' (the fiscal year number followed by '-CLOSE'), so 2025-03-27 and 2026-03-31 are 'FY2025-CLOSE' and 'FY2026-CLOSE'. 26 March is still Q4 and 1 April starts Q1 of the next fiscal year.

Whenever fiscal_label is given a date that does not exist (2024-02-30, 2023-02-29, 2026-02-30, month 13, month 00), it returns the text 'INVALID' instead of NULL or an error, while a real leap day such as 2024-02-29 is accepted and labelled 'FY2024-Q4'.

Whenever fiscal_label is given text that is not in the exact form of four-digit year, two-digit month and two-digit day separated by hyphens (2024-1-5, 2024/04/01, 20240401, empty text, a number, or NULL), it returns NULL; spaces around a valid date are ignored. The exception is a date with a time of day after it (for example '2026-04-01 10:00' or '2026-04-01T10:00:00'): the time is ignored and the label comes from the date part alone, so '2026-04-01 10:00' is 'FY2027-Q1'. The date part must still be in the exact four-digit year, two-digit month, two-digit day form, and a date part that does not exist still returns 'INVALID' whatever time follows it.
Whenever fiscal_label is given an extreme year, it still applies the same rule without a range check: year 0001 gives 'FY2-Q1' with no zero padding, and 9999-12-31 gives 'FY10000-Q3'.

Whenever meeting_end is given a start time and a number of minutes, it rounds the duration up to a whole number of 15-minute blocks (see rule 40) and returns the start plus those rounded minutes as HH:MM on the 24-hour clock with zero padding ('09:00' plus 60 gives '10:00', '9:05' plus 30 gives '09:35', '09:00' plus 45.9 gives '10:00').

Whenever a booking runs past midnight, meeting_end must never wrap around to the next day's clock time, however long the booking is, including a booking of more than 24 hours that would otherwise wrap past midnight a second time. The end is the start plus the minutes, counted straight on without wrapping. Any meeting_end past 23:59, or exactly 24:00, gives '23:59'. For example, '23:30' plus 60 gives '23:59', 1440 minutes gives '23:59', 1500 minutes gives '23:59', and '23:30' plus 25 hours (1500 minutes) gives '23:59', not '00:30'.

Whenever meeting_end is given zero or negative minutes (a duration of zero or less), the duration adds nothing: it never counts backwards from the start and never wraps to the previous evening. The result is the start itself as HH:MM on the 24-hour clock with zero padding ('09:00' minus 30 gives '09:00', '10:00' minus 30 gives '10:00', '00:10' minus 30 gives '00:10', '9:05' minus 10 gives '09:05', '09:00' plus 0 gives '09:00').

Whenever meeting_end is given a start that is not H:MM or HH:MM with two-digit minutes (24:00, 12:60, '9am', '09:00:00', '9:5', empty text, a number, or NULL), it returns NULL; one or two digit hours and spaces around the start are accepted.
Whenever meeting_end is given NULL minutes, it returns NULL.

Whenever meeting_end is given minutes with a fraction or any amount that is not a whole number of 15-minute blocks, it rounds the duration up to the next whole 15-minute block; it never drops the part-minute or the part-block (45 gives 3 blocks, which is 45 minutes; 45.9 gives 4 blocks, which is 60 minutes; 46 gives 60 minutes; 0.5 gives 1 block, which is 15 minutes; an exact multiple of 15 such as 30 or 60 stays as it is). Zero minutes stays zero, and zero or negative durations are still handled by rule 37, so they add nothing. Numeric text such as '30' or '1e2' is read as a number and then rounded up the same way, and text that begins with a number ('30 min') uses that number. Text that is not a number and does not begin with a number ('abc', empty text) is not a duration at all, so meeting_end returns NULL instead of treating it as 0 minutes.

Whenever pct_change is given an old and a new value, it returns (new minus old) divided by the old value itself (with its sign), times 100, rounded to 1 decimal, as a decimal number: 100 to 150 is 50.0 and 150 to 100 is -33.3.

Whenever pct_change is given a negative old value, it divides by the old value with its sign kept, so a rise from a negative old value reads as negative and a fall reads as positive (-100 to -50 is -50.0, -100 to 50 is -150.0).

Whenever pct_change is given an old value of 0, it returns 0.0, whatever the new value is (0 to 50 is 0.0, and 0 to 0 is 0.0); with any other old value, a new value of 0 gives -100.0, and no change gives 0.0.
Whenever pct_change is given a NULL for either value, it returns NULL.

Whenever pct_change is given numeric text such as '100' or ' 100 ', it uses the number; text starting with a number ('150abc') uses the leading number; text that does not start with a number (such as 'abc') or is empty is not a number, so it returns NULL, whether that text is the old value, the new value, or both (so an old value of 100 with a new value of 'abc' gives NULL, an old value of 'abc' with a new value of 100 gives NULL, and 'abc' for both gives NULL). Such text is never treated as zero, on either side, so a new value of 'abc' never gives -100.0.
Whenever pct_change is given a binary (blob) value for either side, it returns NULL.

Whenever the pct_change result falls exactly halfway at the second decimal, it rounds away from zero (2000 to 2001 gives 0.1, 2000 to 1999 gives -0.1), but values that are only a hair below the halfway point because of decimal inexactness round down (100 to 100.05 gives 0.0).

Whenever phone_fmt is given a phone number with 10 digits, it ignores every non-digit character (brackets, hyphens, dots, spaces, plus sign, even letters or surrounding words) and returns it as (AAA) EEE-NNNN ('212.555.1234' and 'call 212-555-1234 now' both give '(212) 555-1234').

Whenever phone_fmt finds 11 digits, whatever the first digit is (including a leading 1), it does not format it and returns the input exactly as it was given ('1-415-555-1234' comes back as '1-415-555-1234', and '+1 212 555 1234' comes back as '+1 212 555 1234'). There is no dropping of a country code.

Whenever phone_fmt is given anything with some other count of digits (7, 9, 12 digits, no digits, empty text, an international number like '+44 20 7946 0958', or non-Western digits), it returns the input exactly as it was given.
Whenever phone_fmt is given NULL, it returns NULL.

Whenever phone_fmt is given a whole number of 10 digits (2125551234), it formats it as text, but a number with a decimal point (2125551234.0), one with too few digits, or one with 11 digits (including one starting with 1) is returned unchanged as a number.
Whenever phone_fmt is given 10 digits, it does not check that the area code or exchange is valid, so '0125551234' gives '(012) 555-1234' and '0000000000' gives '(000) 000-0000'.

Whenever avg_rating is applied to a group of rows, it returns the average of the ratings between 1 and 5 inclusive, always rounded to 1 decimal place, including when the average is a long or repeating decimal (ratings 4 and 5 give 4.5, 5, 4 and 3.5 give 4.2, 5, 3, 1 and 2.5 give 2.9, and 5, 4 and 4 give 4.3, not 4.333333333333333).

Whenever a group has no ratings that count (no rows, all NULL, empty text, or all outside 1 to 5), avg_rating returns NULL.

Whenever avg_rating is used with GROUP BY, it gives one average per group, and without GROUP BY it averages across all selected rows; it is not available on a single value outside a group of rows (avg_rating(5) gives NULL).

rules: Whenever bulk_price is given a unit price and a quantity of fewer than 10, it returns unit price times quantity with no discount, except that a total below the 500-cent minimum order total is raised to 500 (15 cents x 3 gives 500).
Whenever bulk_price is given a quantity of 10 to 49, it takes 5% off the whole order (not just the units above 10), so 10 units at 100 cents cost 950.

Whenever bulk_price is given a quantity of 100 or more, it takes 15% off the whole order. When it is given a quantity of 50 to 99, it takes 10% off the whole order, so 50 units at 100 cents cost 4500.

Whenever a bulk_price discount leaves a fraction of a cent, bulk_price rounds half a cent up to the next whole cent (15 cents x 10 units gives 143 and 3 x 10 gives 29 before the minimum order total is applied; the minimum then raises both to 500).
Whenever bulk_price is given a quantity of zero or less, or a negative unit price, it returns 0 rather than a negative or error value.
Whenever either input to bulk_price is NULL, empty text, or any text (even '100' or '5'), bulk_price returns NULL; only real numbers are accepted, and this check comes before the zero/negative rule.

Whenever bulk_price is given a fractional quantity or price and no discount applies, it drops the fraction of the total, and then applies the 500-cent minimum order total (10.5 cents x 3 gives 31 and 100 x 2.5 gives 250, so both come back as 500, while 100 x 9.99 gives 999).

Whenever bulk_price is given a fractional quantity of 10 or more or a fractional unit price with a discount, the discount tier is judged on the exact quantity (10.5 counts as 10 or more) and the discounted total is rounded half up, though it may come back in decimal form such as 998.0.

Whenever late_fee is given an invoice that is 5 days late or fewer (including zero or negative days), the fee is 0. The grace period is 5 days, so an invoice that is more than 5 days late is chargeable.

Rule 10: Whenever late_fee is given an invoice, the fee is worked out as 2% of the invoice amount per started 30-day period, after a 5-day grace. An invoice that is more than 5 and up to 30 days late is one period (2%; 30 days late is chargeable, not free). An invoice that is 31 to 60 days late is two periods (4%). The 500 cents (5.00 dollars) is only a minimum, not a maximum: the fee for a chargeable invoice is never less than 500 cents, but it is not limited to 500 cents. When the percentage amount is more than 500 cents, the fee is that percentage amount. The cap of 20% of the invoice amount is kept as before and it always wins: the fee is never more than 20% of the invoice amount, even when that is less than 500 cents. So the fee is the percentage amount raised to at least 500 cents, and then limited to the 20% cap (a 12-cent invoice that is 45 days late owes 2 cents, the capped amount).

Whenever late_fee is given an invoice that is 61 or more days late, the percentage is 2% of the whole invoice amount for each started 30-day period, so 61 to 90 days late is 6%, 91 to 120 days late is 8%, and so on, not in addition to the 4%. The percentage keeps rising by 2% for every further started 30-day period, with no stopping point at 6% or any other band, until the 20% cap applies (more than 270 days late). The 500 cents (5.00 dollars) is only a minimum: the percentage amount is raised to at least 500 cents for a chargeable invoice, but the fee is never more than the 20% cap of the invoice amount, and the cap wins over the minimum. For example, a 100-dollar invoice paid 61 days late owes 6.00 dollars (6% of 100 is already above the minimum and below the cap), a 10-dollar invoice paid 61 days late owes 2.00 dollars (the minimum of 5.00 is cut down to the 20% cap), and a 10,000-dollar invoice paid more than a year late owes the 20% cap, 2,000 dollars.

Whenever a late_fee percentage leaves a fraction of a cent, late_fee rounds half a cent up, so 4% of 12 cents is 0 and 4% of 13 cents is 1. This rounding is done on the percentage amount before the minimum and the cap are applied. The cap of 20% of the invoice amount is also rounded half a cent up to a whole cent (20% of 12 cents is 2.4, so the cap is 2 cents). For a chargeable invoice (more than 5 days late, amount above zero) the rounded percentage amount is raised to a minimum of 500 cents (5.00 dollars), and the result is then limited to the 20% cap, so the cap wins over the 500 cents: the fee is never more than the cap, however small the invoice (a 12-cent invoice that is 45 days late owes 2 cents). There is no maximum of 500 cents: when the rounded percentage amount is more than 500 cents, that amount is the fee, unless the 20% cap is lower. Invoices that are not chargeable still owe 0.
Whenever late_fee is given an invoice amount of zero or less, the fee is 0, whatever the days late.

Whenever late_fee is given a fractional days_late, it applies the same limits to the exact value (30.5 days is already in the 4% band, 60.5 days in the 6% band), and a fractional amount gives a whole-cent fee: the percentage amount is rounded to a whole cent first (100.5 cents at 4% gives 4), then raised to the minimum of 500 cents for a chargeable invoice, and then limited to the 20% cap, rounded half a cent up to a whole cent, which wins over the minimum as in the other rules. So a chargeable invoice with a fractional amount or fractional days owes the percentage amount raised to at least 500 cents but never more than the cap (a chargeable invoice of 100.5 cents owes 20 cents, the cap of 20.1 rounded), and more than 500 cents when the rounded percentage amount is higher and within the cap.
Whenever either input to late_fee is NULL, empty text or text of any kind (even '1000' or '40'), late_fee returns NULL, even when the amount is zero or the days are negative.

The total is added and the digit that brings it to a multiple of 11 is returned as text, with 'X' if that digit would be 10 (12345678 gives '6'). A decimal such as 30640615.0 still returns NULL.

Whenever fiscal_label is given a valid YYYY-MM-DD date, the fiscal year starts on 1 April and is named for the calendar year it ends in, so 2024-04-01 is 'FY2025-Q1' and 2025-03-31 is 'FY2025-CLOSE' (31 March is in the year-end close period, so it is labelled CLOSE instead of a quarter).

Whenever fiscal_label is given a date, quarters run Q1 April-June, Q2 July-September, Q3 October-December and Q4 January 1 to March 30, so 2024-06-30 is Q1, 2024-07-01 is Q2, 2024-10-01 is Q3 and 2025-01-01 is Q4; the label looks like 'FY2025-Q1'. The one exception is 31 March of any year, the last day of the fiscal year, which is in the year-end close period and is labelled 'CLOSE' in place of a quarter, in the form 'FY2026-CLOSE' (so 2026-03-31 is 'FY2026-CLOSE', not 'FY2026-Q4'). 30 March and every other day keep their quarter.

Whenever fiscal_label is given a date that does not exist (2024-02-30, 2023-02-29, 2026-02-30, month 13, month 00), it returns the label 'INVALID' (not NULL and not blank), while a real leap day such as 2024-02-29 is accepted and labelled 'FY2024-Q4'.

Whenever fiscal_label is given text whose date part is not in the exact form of four-digit year, two-digit month and two-digit day separated by hyphens (2024-1-5, 2024/04/01, 20240401, empty text, a number, or NULL), it returns NULL; spaces around a valid date are ignored. A valid date followed by a time of day (for example '2026-04-01 09:30') is not rejected: the time is ignored and the label is worked out from the date part alone by the same rules, so '2026-04-01 09:30' is 'FY2027-Q1' and a time on 31 March is still 'CLOSE'. If the date part of such text is in the right form but does not exist (for example '2024-02-30 09:30'), it returns 'INVALID', the same as a date without a time.
Whenever fiscal_label is given an extreme year, it still applies the same rule without a range check: year 0001 gives 'FY2-Q1' with no zero padding, and 9999-12-31 gives 'FY10000-Q3'.

Whenever meeting_end is given a start time and a number of minutes, it returns the start plus those minutes as HH:MM on the 24-hour clock with zero padding ('09:00' plus 60 gives '10:00', '9:05' plus 30 gives '09:35').

Whenever a booking runs past midnight, meeting_end must never wrap around to the next day's clock time, however many hours or days it runs. The start plus the minutes is counted in full, without dropping whole days. Any meeting_end past 23:59, or exactly 24:00, gives '23:59'. For example, '23:30' plus 60 gives '23:59', 1440 minutes gives '23:59', and 1500 minutes gives '23:59'. A 25-hour booking starting at '9:00' (1500 minutes) gives '23:59', not '10:00'. This applies to positive minutes only; negative minutes still follow rule 37.

Whenever meeting_end is given negative minutes, nothing is added and it never counts backwards: the meeting ends at its start time, returned as HH:MM on the 24-hour clock with zero padding ('09:00' minus 30 gives '09:00', '9:00' minus 30 gives '09:00', '10:00' minus 30 gives '10:00', '00:10' minus 30 gives '00:10'). It never ends before it starts and never wraps to the previous evening, however large the negative number. Minutes with a fraction, such as -45.9, are still cut toward zero first (rule 40), and the result is the start time.

Whenever meeting_end is given a start that is not H:MM or HH:MM with two-digit minutes (24:00, 12:60, '9am', '09:00:00', '9:5', empty text, a number, or NULL), it returns NULL; one or two digit hours and spaces around the start are accepted.
Whenever meeting_end is given NULL minutes, it returns NULL.

Whenever meeting_end is given minutes with a fraction, a part minute counts as a started block. For positive minutes, any fraction rounds the duration up to the next whole hour (45.9 gives 60 minutes, so '9:00' plus 45.9 ends at '10:00'; 60.5 gives 120 minutes). Minutes with no fraction are used as they are (45 stays 45). For negative minutes with a fraction, the fraction is still dropped toward zero (-45.9 gives -45), and rule 37 then applies. Numeric text such as '30' or '1e2' is read as a number, and a fraction in it is treated the same way ('45.9' counts as 60 minutes). Text that begins with a number ('30 min') uses that number. Text with no leading number, or empty text, counts as 0 minutes.

Whenever pct_change is given an old and a new value, it returns (new minus old) divided by the old value itself, with its sign kept, times 100, rounded to 1 decimal, as a decimal number: 100 to 150 is 50.0 and 150 to 100 is -33.3.

Whenever pct_change is given a negative old value, it divides by the old value with its sign kept, so the sign of the result flips compared with a positive old value and a rise reads as negative (-100 to -50 is -50.0, -100 to 50 is -150.0).

Whenever pct_change is given an old value of 0, it returns 0.0, whatever the new value is (0 to 50 is 0.0, and 0 to 0 is 0.0); a new value of 0 with a nonzero old value gives -100.0, and no change gives 0.0.
Whenever pct_change is given a NULL for either value, it returns NULL.

Whenever pct_change is given numeric text such as '100' or ' 100 ', it uses the number; text that does not start with a number or is empty counts as 0, so an old value of that kind gives 0.0 and a new value of that kind (with a nonzero old value) gives -100.0; text starting with a number ('150abc') uses the leading number.
Whenever pct_change is given a binary (blob) value for either side, it returns NULL.

Whenever the pct_change result falls exactly halfway at the second decimal, it rounds away from zero (2000 to 2001 gives 0.1, 2000 to 1999 gives -0.1), but values that are only a hair below the halfway point because of decimal inexactness round down (100 to 100.05 gives 0.0).

Whenever phone_fmt is given a phone number with 10 digits, it ignores every non-digit character (brackets, hyphens, dots, spaces, plus sign, even letters or surrounding words) and returns it as (AAA) EEE-NNNN ('212.555.1234' and 'call 212-555-1234 now' both give '(212) 555-1234').

Whenever phone_fmt finds 11 digits, whatever the first digit is (including a leading 1 country code, as in '+1 212 555 1234'), it does not format it and returns the input exactly as it was given. The leading 1 is not dropped.

Whenever phone_fmt is given anything with some other count of digits (7, 9, 12 digits, no digits, empty text, an international number like '+44 20 7946 0958', or non-Western digits), it returns the input exactly as it was given.
Whenever phone_fmt is given NULL, it returns NULL.

Whenever phone_fmt is given a whole number of 10 digits (2125551234), it formats it as text. A number with a decimal point (2125551234.0), a number with 11 digits (even one starting with 1), or one with too few digits is returned unchanged as a number.
Whenever phone_fmt is given 10 digits, it does not check that the area code or exchange is valid, so '0125551234' gives '(012) 555-1234' and '0000000000' gives '(000) 000-0000'.

Whenever avg_rating is applied to a group of rows, it returns the average of the ratings between 1 and 5 inclusive, rounded to 1 decimal place, with halves rounded up (ratings 4 and 5 give 4.5, 4.5 and 3 give 3.8, and 5, 3, 1, 2.5 give 2.9).
Whenever a row's rating is NULL, below 1, above 5, or text (even '4'), avg_rating leaves it out of the average completely, counting neither its value nor the row.
Whenever a group has no ratings that count (no rows, all NULL, empty text, or all outside 1 to 5), avg_rating returns NULL.

Whenever avg_rating is used with GROUP BY, it gives one average per group, and without GROUP BY it averages across all selected rows; it is not available on a single value outside a group of rows (avg_rating(5) gives NULL).
